promptText: For an infinite-scrolling feed, why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset-based pagination?
options: Offset pagination breaks (duplicates or skips rows) when items are inserted or deleted between requests, while cursors stay stable
Cursor pagination is always faster to implement on the client
Offset pagination cannot be cached by a CDN
Cursors eliminate the need for a database index
explanation: New posts arriving or being deleted shifts array offsets, causing offset pagination to duplicate or skip items; cursor-based pagination anchors to a stable position regardless of insertions.

promptText: What is the recommended way to trigger loading the next page in an infinite-scroll list?
options: An IntersectionObserver sentinel placed near the end of the list
A window scroll event listener checking scrollTop on every pixel of movement
A setInterval that polls for new content every second
Fetching the entire dataset upfront on first render
explanation: An IntersectionObserver with a rootMargin buffer triggers the next page fetch efficiently without the performance cost of a dense scroll-event listener firing on every pixel.

promptText: Why should fetched API data (server state) be kept separate from global client state like Redux?
options: Server state has caching, staleness, refetching, and dedup needs that a dedicated data layer (e.g., TanStack Query) handles far better than a generic store
Server state never changes after the initial fetch
Global client state stores data faster than any query library can
There's no real difference; it's purely a stylistic preference
explanation: Treating fetched data as server state with its own caching/invalidation layer avoids the common architectural mistake of manually stuffing API responses into a generic global store.

promptText: Why must optimistic UI updates be paired with a rollback mechanism?
options: The UI is updated before the server confirms the change, so a failed request must revert the local update to stay consistent
Optimistic updates are inherently incorrect and always need correcting
Rollback is a GraphQL-only requirement, not relevant to REST
Rollback is only used for handling race conditions in typeahead search
explanation: Optimistic UI applies the expected result immediately for responsiveness; if the mutation fails server-side, the client must roll back to the previous state or the UI drifts from reality.

promptText: Which rendering strategy is generally best for a private, authenticated dashboard where SEO is irrelevant?
options: CSR (client-side rendering)
SSG (static site generation)
ISR (incremental static regeneration)
Fully static HTML with no client-side JavaScript at all
explanation: Behind a login, SEO doesn't matter, so shifting rendering work to the client (CSR) is an acceptable trade-off, saving server compute that SSR/SSG would otherwise spend on content nobody needs indexed.

promptText: Why should loading, empty, and error states be treated as first-class parts of every async data view?
options: Designing only the happy path is a sign of an incomplete, junior-level design; real data views must handle all three states explicitly
They are mandatory syntax required by React itself
They primarily exist to reduce JavaScript bundle size
They replace the need for accessibility testing entirely
explanation: Volunteering loading/empty/error handling unprompted is a concrete habit interviewers associate with maturity — juniors typically design only the successful data-loaded case.

promptText: In a typeahead/autocomplete search box, why can a race condition occur, and what's a standard fix?
options: A slow response to an earlier keystroke can arrive after a newer one's response; keying results by the query string (or using AbortController to cancel stale requests) ensures only the latest query's data renders
Race conditions only happen on the server, never in client-side search
Debouncing alone, with no other mechanism, fully eliminates the race condition
The fix is to remove all caching from the search requests
explanation: Debouncing reduces request volume but doesn't guarantee response order; keying the query by its exact input value (so a stale key's data is ignored) or aborting superseded requests is what actually prevents the race.

promptText: Why is row virtualization still valuable for a data table showing only a single "page" of a few hundred rows?
options: Rendering hundreds of DOM rows/cells still costs real paint and layout time; virtualization keeps only visible rows in the DOM regardless of how large a "page" is
Virtualization only matters once a dataset exceeds a million rows
Virtualization replaces the need for server-side pagination entirely
Virtualization is a technique exclusively for images, not table rows
explanation: Even a few hundred fully-rendered rows carry meaningful DOM and layout cost; a row virtualizer windows the rendered set to what's actually visible, independent of the server-side page size.

promptText: In a server-evaluated feature-flag architecture, why must the client hydrate using the exact same resolved flag values instead of re-evaluating flags itself?
options: Re-evaluating on the client could produce a different result than what the server used to render the HTML, causing a React hydration mismatch
Client-side flag evaluation runs faster than reading a serialized value
Flags cannot technically be serialized into an HTML payload
Re-evaluating flags client-side is not supported by any framework
explanation: If the server resolves flags once per request and the client re-evaluates independently, a differing result between the two produces a React hydration mismatch; the resolved values must be serialized and reused as-is.

promptText: Why is fractional/lexicographic rank-based positioning preferred over array-index storage for a drag-and-drop Kanban board?
options: A single card's move only requires updating that card's own rank, instead of rewriting and re-broadcasting every card's array index
It removes the need for any backend persistence layer
It guarantees two users can never drag the same card at the same time
It is a strict requirement for keyboard-accessible reordering to function
explanation: Fractional indexing lets you compute a new sort key between two neighbors without renumbering the rest of the list, turning a move into an O(1) update instead of rewriting every card's index.

promptText: Why have most new collaborative rich-text editors moved toward CRDTs instead of Operational Transformation (OT)?
options: CRDTs merge concurrent edits deterministically without needing a central server to sequence operations, unlike OT
CRDTs render text visually faster than OT-based editors
OT is fundamentally incapable of handling plain text editing
CRDTs remove the need for any network synchronization between clients
explanation: OT requires a central authority to sequence and transform operations correctly; CRDTs make each edit self-describing so it merges correctly regardless of arrival order, which is why libraries like Yjs/Automerge are now the default choice.

promptText: In a collaborative editor, why should cursor/selection presence data be handled separately from the durable document content path?
options: Presence is ephemeral, high-frequency state that doesn't need persistence, unlike content which must be durably saved and reliably synced
Presence data must always use a different network protocol for legal reasons
Presence data has to be written in a different programming language than content
There's no functional reason; it's an arbitrary convention with no benefit
explanation: Cursor position and selection change many times per second and expire on disconnect, so routing them through the same durable-persistence path as document content would be wasteful and unnecessary.

promptText: A checkout flow generates an idempotency key once per checkout attempt. A user's network times out after a charge actually succeeded server-side, and the client automatically retries the submit. What actually prevents a double charge, and why is disabling the submit button alone insufficient?
options: The idempotency key makes the retried request a no-op server-side regardless of client state; disabling the button doesn't stop a client-level automatic retry or a fast double-tap that occurs before the disabled state applies
The browser automatically blocks duplicate network requests to the same URL
Disabling the submit button on click is fully sufficient by itself
Idempotency keys only work for GET requests, not payment charges
explanation: The idempotency key is the actual correctness guarantee — the backend recognizes a repeated key as a no-op — because a UI-level guard like a disabled button can be bypassed by a fast double-tap or an automatic client retry.

promptText: A dashboard has 20+ widgets; two of them independently query overlapping "sales" data with the same date range and filters. What architectural choice avoids redundant requests, and what's the downside of skipping it?
options: Route requests through a shared query cache keyed by the actual parameters so identical requests dedupe; without it, teams end up hammering the same endpoint redundantly and often paper over it with bespoke aggregation endpoints
Add a dedicated backend endpoint tailored to every possible widget combination
Increase the polling interval uniformly across all widgets regardless of freshness needs
There is no real downside since browsers cache identical GET requests automatically in all cases
explanation: A shared query cache keyed by (metric, range, filters) lets two widgets needing the same data slice dedupe into one request; skipping this leads to redundant load and ad hoc backend workarounds instead of fixing the data layer.

promptText: A CDN caches HTML by URL, but a new feature is gated behind a percentage-based rollout flag. What is the core tension this creates, and what are the two typical resolutions?
options: A URL-only cache key would serve identical HTML to every user regardless of their flag bucket; teams either fragment the cache key by cohort (at some cache-hit-rate cost) or push the flag-gated content into a small dynamic, client-rendered island
The tension resolves automatically without any configuration on any CDN
Feature flags cannot be used at all on any CDN-cached page
The only fix is disabling the CDN entirely for the whole site
explanation: A shared CDN cache keyed only by URL can't distinguish flag cohorts; fragmenting the cache key (trading some hit-rate) or isolating the variable content to a client-rendered island are the two real resolutions to this trade-off.
